 Assessing the Threat: Election interference attempts from outside, within US 
 Officials prepared for 2026 midterm election interference attempts from outside and within the US. WLS By Mark Rivera , Barb Markoff, Christine Tressel and Tom Jones Saturday, November 7, 2026 12:47AM Share CHICAGO (WLS) -- States across the country have been on high alert for election interference by foreign threats, and threats from within, officials told the ABC7 I-Team.
 And even though Election Day has passed seemingly successfully, a former U.S. Department of Homeland Security intelligence chief told the I-Team this year states prepared for a new threat from within and potential efforts to undermine the results of the midterm elections.

 "A number of states prepared for efforts to interfere with the voting process, not by criminals or foreign threat actors, but by organizations associated with the federal government," said John Cohen, former DHS intelligence chief and ABC News contributor.
 Cohen told the I-Team preparations by local officials for election interference during the midterms were essential.
 "We saw several states impacted by cyberattacks that took down their websites. We actually saw several examples where threat actors sent inaccurate text messages regarding location and time for voting to people," Cohen said. "We saw multiple bomb threats at locations in various states."
 The Illinois Statewide Terrorism and Intelligence Center told the I-Team there were no reports of election disruption, interference or attempts to interfere with voting this year.

 But Cohen said there was another insidious potential threat in 2026: a threat from within the United States itself. It's something Cohen says he's never seen before in more than four decades in law enforcement and with Homeland Security.
 "The fact that they were even taking steps to address the potentiality of that type of activity is a pretty strong statement," Cohen said.
 Democrats secured major victories nationwide despite efforts from the U.S. Department of Justice to preemptively challenge ballots on the unverified suspicion there would be widespread illegal voting: a claim from the Trump administration that has consistently been disproven.
 Now, the administration may attempt once again to challenge votes cast.
 This week, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the agency will be "gathering voting logs" to ensure nobody voted illegally.
 "That belief can't stem from conspiracy theories or conjecture or someone's political objectives. It has to be based on credible information that leads one to reasonably believe that a crime has or is about to be committed," Cohen said. "Using those tools to gather information for political purposes is in violation of a number of federal laws."
 Cohen believes the midterm election sent a strong statement to the federal government and the Departments of Homeland Security and Justice that Americans want an end to highly polarized use of federal resources.
